name: Snatch / Press
description: A one-arm kettlebell snatch immediately followed by a strict overhead press, performed as a single combination rep before switching arms.
benefits: Builds explosive hip drive
Develops overhead stability under fatigue
Trains grip endurance
commonMistakes: Muscling the snatch with the arm instead of driving with the hips
Pressing with an arched lower back instead of a braced core
Letting the bell crash into the rack position

name: Clean / Squat
description: A kettlebell clean into the rack position, followed by a front squat with the bell held at the shoulder.
benefits: Combines a hip-hinge pull with a squat pattern
Reinforces a stable front-rack position
Builds full-body coordination under load
commonMistakes: Banging the wrist on the clean instead of a smooth rack
Letting the knees cave inward on the squat
Losing the upright torso as fatigue sets in

name: Swing
description: A two-handed hip-hinge movement that projects the kettlebell forward using explosive hip extension, not the arms.
benefits: Foundational hip-hinge and posterior chain builder
High-output conditioning with low joint impact
Teaches explosive hip extension used across every other kettlebell lift
commonMistakes: Squatting the swing instead of hinging at the hips
Lifting the bell with the arms and shoulders
Overextending the lower back at the top instead of standing tall

name: Deadlift Side
description: A single-kettlebell deadlift performed with the bell positioned outside the foot rather than centered, adding an anti-rotation demand.
benefits: Builds hip-hinge strength unilaterally
Trains anti-rotation core stability
Carries over to real-world asymmetric lifting
commonMistakes: Rounding the spine to reach the bell
Letting the hips rotate toward the kettlebell
Rushing the lockout instead of standing fully tall

name: Farmer Carry
description: Walking a fixed distance while carrying one or two kettlebells at the sides with a tall, braced posture.
benefits: Builds raw grip endurance
Reinforces postural strength under load
Simple, brutally effective conditioning tool
commonMistakes: Letting the shoulders round forward
Taking short, hurried steps instead of a controlled pace
Leaning to one side with an uneven load

name: Alternating Snatch
description: The one-arm kettlebell snatch performed for reps, alternating arms at a set interval rather than staying on one side.
benefits: Full-body power development
Trains fast, repeated hip extension
Builds grip and shoulder stamina evenly on both sides
commonMistakes: Muscling the bell up instead of driving from the hips
Catching the bell hard on the wrist instead of 'punching through'
Losing tension in the midsection between reps

name: Renegade Row
description: A plank position with hands on two kettlebells, rowing one bell to the ribs at a time while resisting rotation.
benefits: Builds anti-rotation core strength
Combines a pulling movement with a stability challenge
Improves shoulder stability under load
commonMistakes: Letting the hips rotate toward the rowing arm
Sagging through the lower back
Rowing with momentum instead of a controlled pull

name: Goblet Squat
description: A squat performed holding a single kettlebell at chest height with both hands, elbows tracking inside the knees.
benefits: Reinforces an upright squat position
Beginner-friendly entry point to loaded squatting
Builds trunk stability against a front-loaded weight
commonMistakes: Letting the heels lift off the ground
Rounding the upper back at the bottom
Not reaching full depth

name: High Pull
description: A two-handed or single-arm explosive pull that drives the kettlebell from hip height up toward chin height, elbow leading.
benefits: Bridges hip-hinge power into an upper-body pull
Builds explosive triple extension
Develops upper-back and shoulder strength
commonMistakes: Pulling with the arm before the hips finish extending
Shrugging instead of driving the elbow high
Using too much weight and losing the pulling path

name: Clean & Press
description: A kettlebell clean into the rack position immediately followed by a strict or push press overhead.
benefits: Classic full-body strength builder
Trains the transition from a hip-driven pull to an overhead push
Builds real-world pressing strength under fatigue
commonMistakes: Pressing with an arched back instead of a braced core
Skipping a clean rack and muscling straight to the shoulder
Losing wrist alignment overhead

name: Front Squat
description: A squat performed with one or two kettlebells held in the rack position at the shoulders.
benefits: Builds squat strength with a demanding upright torso requirement
Reinforces the rack position used in cleans and presses
Strong core and postural carryover
commonMistakes: Letting the elbows drop, collapsing the rack
Leaning forward to compensate for a loose core
Cutting the squat short of full depth

name: Double Clean
description: A simultaneous two-kettlebell clean, bringing both bells from the floor or a hang position into a double rack.
benefits: Builds symmetrical full-body power
Heavier total load than single-bell work
Strong grip and rack-position demand
commonMistakes: Letting one side lag behind the other
Banging both wrists on the rack instead of a smooth catch
Rounding the back on the pull from the floor

name: Double Press
description: A strict or push press of two kettlebells simultaneously from the rack position to full lockout overhead.
benefits: Heavy bilateral pressing strength
Demands serious core bracing to keep the ribs down
Builds shoulder stability at heavier total loads
commonMistakes: Flaring the ribs and arching the lower back
Pressing unevenly, favoring the stronger side
Losing braced tension between reps

name: Double Front Squat
description: A front squat performed holding two kettlebells in the rack position, one at each shoulder.
benefits: Heaviest common double-kettlebell squat variation
Severe core and upper-back bracing demand
Builds serious total-body squat capacity
commonMistakes: Letting the elbows drift down and forward
Losing depth as fatigue accumulates
Leaning forward instead of sitting straight down

name: Double Snatch
description: Two kettlebells driven from the hang to lockout overhead in one explosive pull — the same snatch as a single bell, doubled, demanding twice the hip power and twice the grip endurance.
benefits: Builds explosive hip drive under bilateral load
Trains grip endurance far beyond single-bell work
Conditions the whole body under real fatigue
commonMistakes: Muscling the bells up with the arms instead of the hips
Letting the bells crash at the bottom of the backswing
Losing lockout timing between the two arms

name: Double Thruster
description: A double-bell front squat that rolls directly into a double overhead press — a single continuous movement that punishes any pause between the two halves.
benefits: Combines a squat and a press into one continuous effort
Builds leg drive that carries directly into the press
Elevates heart rate quickly — a full-body conditioning tool
commonMistakes: Pausing at the top of the squat before pressing
Losing rack position on the way down
Pressing with the arms alone instead of riding the leg drive

name: Thruster
description: The single-bell version of the front squat into overhead press — same continuous demand, with an added anti-rotation challenge from carrying the load on one side.
benefits: Builds single-side leg drive and pressing power together
Trains anti-rotation core strength from the offset load
Cheap on equipment, expensive on the lungs
commonMistakes: Letting the offset load pull the torso sideways
Stalling between the squat and the press
Rushing the rack position and losing wrist alignment

name: Bent-over Row
description: A hinged-position row, pulling the bell(s) from a straight-arm hang to the ribs — a grind movement that demands a locked, neutral spine under load.
benefits: Builds pulling strength to balance the pressing/snatching volume elsewhere
Trains hip-hinge positional strength under time
Strengthens the posterior chain that carries and presses depend on
commonMistakes: Rounding the lower back to finish the pull
Using momentum instead of a controlled pull
Standing up out of the hinge between reps

name: Front Rack Carry
description: Two kettlebells held in the front rack position while walking a set distance — a loaded carry that punishes any break in bracing before it punishes the legs.
benefits: Builds total-body bracing strength under sustained load
Trains the rack position to hold under fatigue, not just for a single rep
Carries over directly into every double-bell lift that starts from the rack
commonMistakes: Letting the elbows drop and the load shift onto the wrists
Shortening the stride to rush the distance
Breathing shallow instead of bracing through the whole carry

name: Tactical Double Snatch
description: A double snatch performed with continuous tension — no dead stop at the bottom, no relaxed lockout at the top — kept technically clean under a descending rep scheme.
benefits: Builds explosive power that stays clean as reps accumulate
Reinforces hip-drive technique under fatigue rather than under fresh conditions
Demands full-body tension from first rep to last
commonMistakes: Letting form drift as the round wears on
Resting at the top instead of maintaining tension
Rushing the descending scheme instead of holding pace

name: Tactical Double Front Squat
description: A double-bell front squat held with strict control through a descending rep scheme — technical precision, not speed, is the whole point.
benefits: Builds squat strength that holds up under real fatigue
Reinforces bracing and rack position technique deep into a round
Trains total-body control rather than raw output
commonMistakes: Letting the chest fall forward as fatigue builds
Losing rack position and shifting weight onto the wrists
Rushing depth to save time instead of holding form

name: Tactical Double Press
description: A strict double overhead press with no leg drive, no momentum — every rep locked out under full control, even as the round wears on.
benefits: Builds raw overhead pressing strength without compensation
Reinforces core bracing needed to press without arching the back
Exposes and corrects left/right imbalance
commonMistakes: Arching the lower back to help the bells overhead
Pressing unevenly between the two arms
Letting the elbows flare instead of pressing in a straight line

name: Tactical Double Clean
description: A controlled double clean into the rack — no bouncing the bells off the chest, no muscling them up sloppy — every rep resetting technique before the next.
benefits: Reinforces clean technique under a demanding rep scheme
Builds the hip-to-rack timing every other double-bell lift depends on
Protects the wrists and forearms by forcing a soft catch every rep
commonMistakes: Letting the bells crash into the forearms on the catch
Muscling the clean up with the arms instead of the hips
Rushing the rack position to save time

name: Snatch
description: A single kettlebell driven from the hang to an overhead lockout in one pull — the foundational ballistic movement every double-bell variation builds on.
benefits: Builds the hip-snap technique every heavier snatch variation depends on
Trains one-sided power and grip endurance
Lower-barrier entry point to the whole snatch family
commonMistakes: Pulling with the arm instead of driving with the hips
Letting the bell crash on the backswing
Punching through the top instead of finishing a soft lockout

name: Press
description: A single kettlebell strict-pressed from the rack to lockout — a pure test of one-sided pressing strength with the core resisting the sideways pull of the load.
benefits: Builds strict overhead pressing strength one side at a time
Exposes left/right strength imbalance early
Trains anti-lateral-flexion core strength from the offset load
commonMistakes: Leaning away from the load instead of bracing against it
Using leg drive on a movement meant to be strict
Pressing behind the frontal plane instead of straight up

name: Clean
description: A single kettlebell pulled from the hang into the rack position — the entry movement for every single-bell pressing and squatting variation.
benefits: Builds the hip-to-rack timing that presses and squats depend on
Trains a soft, controlled catch that protects the wrist
Foundational movement for every heavier clean variation
commonMistakes: Letting the bell bang into the forearm on the catch
Curling the bell up with the arm instead of snapping the hips
Catching with a bent wrist instead of a stacked one

name: Double Half Snatch
description: A double-bell snatch stopped at the rack instead of finishing overhead — the explosive pull of a snatch without the final lockout, repeated under fatigue.
benefits: Builds hip power without adding overhead-lockout fatigue to already-tired shoulders
Bridges cleanly between clean and snatch technique
Lets a long round keep moving without a full overhead reset every rep
commonMistakes: Letting the pull die early and muscling the rest with the arms
Catching too high or too low in the rack
Losing bracing between reps

name: Reverse Lunge
description: A single-leg step-back lunge, performed under a double-bell load — a lower-body movement that demands balance as much as strength when everything else in the round is upper-body and hips.
benefits: Adds real single-leg strength work into an otherwise hip-dominant complex
Builds balance and control under load, not just raw output
Gives the grip and shoulders a brief recovery window mid-round without stopping the clock
commonMistakes: Letting the front knee cave inward on the way up
Taking too short a step and losing balance
Rushing the rep count instead of controlling the descent

name: Double Push Press
description: A double-bell press assisted by a short dip and drive from the legs — more weight overhead, faster, by borrowing power from the legs instead of the shoulders alone.
benefits: Moves more overhead load than a strict press by sharing the work with the legs
Builds the timing between leg drive and the overhead lockout
Keeps shoulders fresher deep into a long round than a strict press would
commonMistakes: Dipping too deep and turning it into a jerk
Mistiming the leg drive so the arms do all the work anyway
Losing the overhead lockout position on the catch

name: Double Swing
description: Two kettlebells swung from between the legs to chest height using the hips — the same hinge-and-snap as a single swing, doubled, with twice the grip demand.
benefits: Trains the hip hinge that every ballistic movement in this campaign depends on
Builds grip and forearm endurance under sustained ballistic load
High output, low technical barrier — sustains pace deep into a round
commonMistakes: Squatting the swing instead of hinging at the hips
Muscling the bells up with the shoulders
Letting the bells drop below the knees on the backswing

name: Double High Pull
description: Two kettlebells pulled explosively from the hang to chest height, elbows leading — a ballistic pull that stops short of the overhead lockout, keeping the pace high.
benefits: Builds the same hip-snap power as a snatch with less overhead fatigue
Trains upper-back and shoulder pulling strength alongside the hips
Keeps a round's pace high without the technical reset a full snatch needs
commonMistakes: Pulling with the arms before the hips finish driving
Letting the elbows drop below the wrists on the pull
Losing rhythm and turning the pull into a shrug

name: Snatch / Thruster
description: A one-arm kettlebell snatch immediately followed by a thruster on the same side, performed as a single combination rep before switching arms.
benefits: Chains a ballistic hip-drive movement into a grinding squat-press
Builds work capacity under a heavier single-bell load
Trains the transition from explosive to controlled effort mid-set
commonMistakes: Resetting the rack position between the snatch and the thruster instead of flowing into it
Letting the squat depth collapse once the shoulders start to fatigue
Losing the overhead lockout on the thruster's press

name: Alternating Swing
description: A single-kettlebell two-hand-style swing performed one arm at a time, passing or switching the bell between hands at the top of each rep instead of staying on one side.
benefits: Trains hip-hinge power evenly on both sides in one continuous set
Builds grip and forearm endurance through the hand-to-hand transition
Keeps the pace of a two-handed swing without loading one side twice as long
commonMistakes: Muscling the switch with the shoulder instead of letting the hip snap drive it
Rounding the lower back to chase the switch timing
Losing the hinge pattern and squatting the swing

name: Switching Swing
description: A single-kettlebell swing performed for a full set on one arm, then handed cleanly to the other arm for an equal set — one deliberate switch mid-exercise, not a swap every rep.
benefits: Trains hip-hinge power to full fatigue on one side before repeating it on the other
Builds grip and forearm endurance across a sustained one-arm set
Reinforces a clean, controlled hand-to-hand transfer instead of a rushed swap
commonMistakes: Switching hands early, before the full count on the working side is done
Rounding the lower back to muscle out the last reps of a side
Losing the hinge pattern and squatting the swing

name: Floor Press
description: A kettlebell press performed lying on the back, elbows touching the floor at the bottom of each rep instead of a standing rack position — a shorter, more controlled range of motion.
benefits: Presses heavy with less shoulder strain than a standing press
Removes the legs entirely, isolating pressing strength
Teaches a stable, controlled lockout without needing to brace against a fall
commonMistakes: Bouncing the elbows off the floor instead of pausing
Flaring the elbows too wide and stressing the shoulder joint
Losing the wrist stack and pressing off-line

name: Plank + KB Pull Through
description: A kettlebell dragged from one side to the other underneath a held plank position, one pull-through per rep, while the hips and shoulders resist rotation.
benefits: Builds anti-rotation core strength under time pressure
Trains shoulder stability under a shifting, off-center load
Keeps grip and core engaged simultaneously through a full round
commonMistakes: Letting the hips rotate or sag toward the pulling arm
Rushing the pull and losing plank alignment
Holding the breath instead of breathing through the hold

name: Snatch / Clean / Jerk
description: A three-part kettlebell complex — one snatch, one clean, one jerk — performed as a single unbroken sequence before resetting for the next rep.
benefits: Chains three distinct hip-drive patterns into one continuous test
Builds overhead stability under accumulating fatigue
Trains the technical reset between three different rack positions
commonMistakes: Rushing the transition between lifts and losing the rack position
Substituting a push press for the jerk's dip-drive-catch
Letting grip fatigue break form before the legs or shoulders do

name: Row / Clean / Thruster
description: A three-part kettlebell complex — one bent-over row, one clean, one thruster — performed as a single unbroken sequence before resetting for the next rep.
benefits: Chains a pulling movement directly into a full-body pressing movement
Builds work capacity across the whole posterior and anterior chain in one sequence
Trains transitioning from a hinged pull straight into a loaded squat
commonMistakes: Rounding the back on the row to rush into the clean
Losing squat depth on the thruster once the row has pre-fatigued the grip
Resetting the kettlebell to the floor between parts instead of flowing through

name: Snatch from the Floor
description: A one-arm kettlebell snatch starting from a dead stop on the floor instead of a hang or backswing, forcing a fresh hip-hinge setup on every single rep.
benefits: Removes momentum from the backswing, isolating raw hip-drive power
Builds a stronger, more repeatable setup position under fatigue
Trains grip strength from a true dead-stop rather than a moving bell
commonMistakes: Yanking the bell up with the arm instead of resetting the hip hinge
Rushing the floor pickup and rounding the lower back
Losing tension between reps instead of treating each one as its own lift

name: Clean from the Floor
description: A one-arm kettlebell clean starting from a dead stop on the floor, resetting the hip hinge completely between reps instead of cycling the bell in a continuous swing.
benefits: Builds a clean, repeatable hip-hinge setup under fatigue
Trains the bell into the rack position without relying on backswing momentum
Develops forearm and grip control from a true dead-stop pickup
commonMistakes: Muscling the bell into the rack instead of driving from the hips
Letting the bell crash into the forearm on the catch
Rounding the back on the floor pickup instead of hinging

name: Clean from the Floor / Thruster
description: A one-arm kettlebell clean starting from a dead stop on the floor, immediately followed by a thruster on the same side before resetting for the next rep.
benefits: Chains a dead-stop pulling movement directly into a full-body squat-press
Builds work capacity from the floor up through a full overhead lockout
Trains the technical reset between a floor pickup and a loaded squat
commonMistakes: Rushing the floor pickup to get to the thruster faster
Letting squat depth collapse once the shoulder starts to fatigue
Losing the overhead lockout on the thruster's press

name: Alternating Double Clean
description: Two kettlebells cleaned to the rack with an alternating tempo — one bell arrives a half-beat ahead of the other — instead of both bells cleaned in a single synchronized motion.
benefits: Trains each side to stabilize independently while the other is still moving
Builds core anti-rotation strength from the offset timing
Keeps the rack transition honest on both sides instead of letting one side lag
commonMistakes: Letting the offset tempo turn into two separate uneven singles
Losing rack tension on the leading arm while catching the trailing one
Rounding the back to rush the timing

name: Alternating Press
description: Two kettlebells pressed overhead one at a time in a left-right-left-right sequence, the resting bell held in the rack while the other presses.
benefits: Builds overhead pressing strength while the core resists the shifting load
Trains one side to stay braced and stable while the other works
Keeps the shoulders under near-continuous tension across the full set
commonMistakes: Letting the resting bell drift out of the rack position
Arching the lower back to finish the press instead of bracing the core
Rushing the side-to-side rhythm and losing lockout on each rep

name: Gorilla Row
description: Two kettlebells set on the floor in a wide hinge stance, rowed one arm at a time in a left-right-left-right sequence while the other hand stays braced on its own bell.
benefits: Builds unilateral pulling strength from a stable, grounded stance
Trains the core and hips to hold a hinge under an offset, shifting load
Keeps grip and back tension high across both sides in one continuous set
commonMistakes: Rotating the torso to muscle the row up instead of pulling with the back
Letting the hips rise and turn the hinge into a squat
Losing bracing tension in the resting arm between reps

name: Jerk
description: A kettlebell driven overhead from the rack with a dip-drive-catch, the feet re-setting under the bell at the top instead of a single continuous press.
benefits: Moves heavier loads overhead than a strict press by using the legs to drive
Trains fast, stable footwork under a loaded overhead catch
Builds overhead lockout strength with less pure shoulder fatigue than pressing
commonMistakes: Turning the dip-drive into a push press with no foot re-set
Catching with a soft, unlocked elbow instead of a stacked lockout
Re-setting the feet too wide or too late under the bell

name: Tactical Snatch
description: A one-arm kettlebell snatch performed at a slower, deliberate tactical tempo — a controlled pause at the top and bottom — rather than the continuous cycling of a standard snatch.
benefits: Removes momentum from the lockout, testing raw shoulder stability
Builds control at both ends of the rep instead of relying on cycling rhythm
Trains grip and shoulder endurance under sustained time-under-tension
commonMistakes: Rushing through the pause and turning it back into a standard snatch
Losing tension in the plank-like brace during the top-position hold
Letting the bell crash instead of lowering it under control

name: Floor Deadlift
description: A kettlebell deadlifted from a dead stop on the floor to standing, hips driving the bell up rather than the arms, resetting fully between reps.
benefits: Builds raw hip-hinge strength from a true dead-stop position
Reinforces a braced, neutral spine under load before any other lift begins
Trains grip and posterior-chain strength together on every rep
commonMistakes: Rounding the lower back to reach the floor instead of hinging at the hips
Yanking the bell up instead of driving through the heels
Losing the reset and turning it into a continuous swing

name: Floor Push
description: A kettlebell cleaned from the floor and pressed overhead in one standing sequence, the bell never resting in the rack before the press begins.
benefits: Chains a floor pickup directly into an overhead lockout without a rack pause
Builds shoulder stability under a load that just arrived, not one that's settled
Trains full-body tension from the floor to full extension in one continuous effort
commonMistakes: Pausing in the rack instead of driving straight through to the press
Arching the lower back to finish the lockout
Losing tension in the picked-up hand while the other stays braced

name: Floor Clean / Push
description: A kettlebell cleaned from a dead stop on the floor, immediately followed by an overhead push before resetting for the next rep.
benefits: Combines a dead-stop pulling movement with an overhead pressing movement in one rep
Builds work capacity from the floor to full lockout without rack rest between reps
Trains the technical reset between a floor pickup and an overhead finish
commonMistakes: Rushing the floor pickup to get to the push faster
Letting the rack position collapse before driving overhead
Losing the overhead lockout at the top of the push

name: Double Jerk
description: Two kettlebells driven overhead together from the rack with a dip-drive-catch, the feet re-setting under both bells at the top instead of a single continuous press.
benefits: Moves heavier total load overhead than a double press by using the legs to drive
Trains fast, stable footwork under a loaded two-bell overhead catch
Builds overhead lockout strength on both sides at once with less pure shoulder fatigue
commonMistakes: Turning the dip-drive into a double push press with no foot re-set
Catching with one side locked out before the other
Re-setting the feet unevenly under an uneven pair of bells

name: Overhead Lunge
description: A reverse or walking lunge performed while holding a kettlebell locked out overhead, the shoulder and core working to keep the bell stacked while the legs step through the lunge.
benefits: Trains overhead shoulder stability under a shifting, moving base
Builds single-leg strength while the core resists lateral lean from the raised load
Carries over to any movement that needs a stable overhead position under fatigue
commonMistakes: Letting the raised arm drift forward or out of the ear-line during the step
Rushing the lunge and losing lockout at the top of the movement
Leaning the torso toward the working leg instead of staying stacked

name: Windmill
description: A kettlebell held locked out overhead while the hips hinge sideways, the free hand reaching toward the floor along the front leg before returning to standing.
benefits: Builds shoulder stability under a static overhead load through a full hip hinge
Trains lateral core strength and hip mobility together in one controlled movement
Reinforces the overhead lockout that other overhead lifts depend on
commonMistakes: Bending the overhead arm instead of keeping it locked throughout
Rounding the lower back to reach further down instead of hinging at the hip
Rushing the return to standing and losing the overhead line

name: Floor Thruster
description: A kettlebell cleaned from a dead stop on the floor directly into a thruster — squat and overhead drive in one motion — before resetting for the next rep.
benefits: Combines a dead-stop floor pickup with a full squat-to-overhead drive in one rep
Builds total-body power output from the ground up with no rack pause
Trains leg drive to carry a load all the way to lockout under fatigue
commonMistakes: Rushing the floor pickup and losing the hip hinge before the squat
Cutting the squat depth short to get to the press faster
Losing the overhead lockout at the top of the drive

name: Burpee → Kettlebell
description: A standard burpee finishing by driving up to grip and clean two kettlebells to the rack, chaining a bodyweight movement directly into the loaded work that follows.
benefits: Builds work capacity by pairing bodyweight and loaded movement without a pause
Trains the transition from the floor to a loaded rack position under fatigue
Raises heart rate fast, testing pacing early in a round
commonMistakes: Standing up out of the burpee before reaching for the bells
Rushing the clean into the rack and losing wrist position
Letting the chest collapse on the way down

name: Long-Hike Snatch
description: A double kettlebell snatch that starts from an exaggerated hike pass well behind the hips before driving both bells overhead in one motion.
benefits: Extends the pulling range for more hip drive per rep
Trains timing between the hike and the upward pull
Builds grip and shoulder stability at lockout
commonMistakes: Cutting the hike short and losing the extra range
Muscling the bells up with the arms instead of the hips
Catching overhead with the wrists rolled back

name: Long-Hike Clean
description: A double kettlebell clean that starts from the same exaggerated hike pass as the Long-Hike Snatch, driving both bells to the rack instead of overhead.
benefits: Extends the pulling range for more hip drive per rep
Builds a soft, controlled catch in the rack from a longer backswing
Reinforces the same hike timing as its Snatch counterpart
commonMistakes: Cutting the hike short and losing the extra range
Catching the rack hard on the wrists and forearms
Letting the bells drift away from the body on the way up

name: Burpee
description: A bodyweight burpee performed directly beside two racked kettlebells, finishing in a standing position ready to pick them straight back up for the next movement.
benefits: Raises heart rate without adding external load, so the following lift is met by cardio fatigue rather than muscular fatigue alone
Reinforces getting up off the floor efficiently between loaded work
Builds the conditioning base the rest of a complex is tested against
commonMistakes: Letting the hips sag on the way down
Popping up too fast and arriving unbalanced for the next pickup
Skipping the full chest-to-floor range under fatigue

name: Clean → Jerk
description: Two kettlebells cleaned to the rack and driven overhead in a single jerk, performed as one continuous couplet before resetting for the next rep.
benefits: Combines a hip-driven pull with an overhead drive in one couplet
Trains the rack-to-overhead transition under accumulating fatigue
Repeats as the workout's recurring technical checkpoint, testing composure as much as output
commonMistakes: Muscling the clean instead of using hip drive, arriving out of position for the jerk
Losing the dip-drive timing on the jerk as fatigue builds
Catching overhead with the bells drifting forward of the ears

name: Deadlift
description: A standard two-kettlebell deadlift — hinge to grip, drive through the floor to lockout, control back down. The baseline hinge pattern, distinct from the Floor Deadlift's dead-stop reset and Deadlift Side's offset stance.
benefits: Reinforces the hip hinge that every ballistic movement in a complex depends on
Builds posterior chain strength and grip endurance without a technical bottleneck
Gives the nervous system a controlled reset between more explosive movements
commonMistakes: Rounding the lower back to make up for a hip hinge that broke down early
Letting the bells drift forward away from the shins
Rushing the lockout instead of finishing tall

name: Deep Snatch
description: A one-arm kettlebell snatch performed from a lower, deeper hike position than a standard Snatch, extending the pull before the bell is driven overhead.
benefits: Extends the pulling range for more hip drive per rep
Demands tighter timing between the deeper hike and the upward pull
Builds grip and shoulder stability at lockout under a longer lever
commonMistakes: Cutting the hike short and losing the extra range it's meant to add
Muscling the bell up with the arm instead of the hips
Catching overhead with the wrist rolled back instead of stacked

name: Floor Pull
description: A single kettlebell pulled explosively off the floor to about hip height with a bent-arm row, then returned to a dead stop for the next rep.
benefits: Builds pulling strength from a true dead stop
Trains the floor as a reset point instead of relying on bell momentum
Reinforces a flat back under a loaded hinge
commonMistakes: Rounding the back to muscle the bell up
Using the hips to heave the bell instead of pulling with the back
Letting the bell drift away from the shins on the way up

name: Suitcase Deadlift
description: A conventional-stance deadlift performed with one kettlebell on one side of the body, resisting the lateral pull with the core for the full set before switching sides.
benefits: Trains anti-lateral-flexion core strength under a loaded hinge
Builds single-side pulling strength without a symmetrical counterbalance
Exposes and corrects hip-level asymmetries a double-bell deadlift can hide
commonMistakes: Leaning toward the loaded side to compensate
Letting the shoulders rotate open toward the bell
Rushing the lockout instead of finishing the hip extension

name: Single-Leg Romanian Deadlift
description: A one-legged hip hinge holding a kettlebell in the opposite hand, lowering the bell toward the floor while the free leg extends back for balance.
benefits: Builds single-leg balance and hip control under load
Isolates hamstring and glute strength on one side at a time
Exposes stability weaknesses a two-footed hinge won't reveal
commonMistakes: Rotating the hips open instead of keeping them square to the floor
Bending the standing knee instead of hinging at the hip
Rushing the balance point instead of controlling the descent

name: Romanian Deadlift
description: A stiff-legged hip hinge lowering the kettlebell along the shins to a hamstring stretch before driving the hips back through to standing.
benefits: Builds posterior-chain strength through a long range of motion
Reinforces hip-hinge mechanics under continuous tension
Develops hamstring control at end range, not just lockout strength
commonMistakes: Squatting the movement instead of hinging at the hips
Losing the flat back as the bell passes the knees
Stopping the descent short of an actual hamstring stretch

name: Single-Arm Clean
description: A single kettlebell pulled from the hinge and guided into the rack position in one motion, absorbing the bell into the forearm rather than catching it.
benefits: Builds the hip-to-rack timing every single-arm complex depends on
Trains the forearm to absorb impact instead of the wrist
Develops explosive hip extension on one side at a time
commonMistakes: Muscling the bell up with the arm instead of the hips
Letting the bell bang into the wrist instead of the forearm
Losing tension in the rack position after the catch

name: Single-Arm Press
description: A strict overhead press of one kettlebell from the rack, driving straight up without leg drive or momentum.
benefits: Builds strict pressing strength on each side independently
Trains anti-lateral-flexion core strength under an offset overhead load
Exposes shoulder or core weaknesses a two-bell press can hide
commonMistakes: Leaning away from the loaded side instead of staying stacked
Flaring the elbow instead of pressing along a straight bar path
Using a leg dip to sneak in momentum

name: Single-Arm Thruster
description: A front squat with one kettlebell in the rack, standing explosively out of the bottom to drive the bell overhead in one continuous motion.
benefits: Combines a loaded single-arm squat with an overhead press under fatigue
Builds leg drive that transfers directly into the overhead lockout
Trains core stability against the offset load of a single bell
commonMistakes: Pausing at the top of the squat instead of driving straight through
Finishing the press with the arm alone instead of leg drive
Letting the torso lean away from the loaded side

name: Double Row
description: A hinged-position row with two kettlebells, pulling both bells from a straight-arm hang to the ribs together — a bilateral grind that loads the whole back at once instead of alternating sides.
benefits: Builds bilateral pulling strength to balance the pressing/snatching volume elsewhere
Trains hip-hinge positional strength under a symmetrical two-bell load
Strengthens the posterior chain that carries and presses depend on
commonMistakes: Rounding the lower back to finish the pull
Using momentum instead of a controlled pull
Standing up out of the hinge between reps

name: Long Cycle
description: Two kettlebells cleaned once, then driven overhead in a jerk for every rep of the set without re-cleaning between reps — the rack is held, not reset.
benefits: Builds overhead pressing endurance under a rack that never gets to reset
Trains hip-drive efficiency across repeated jerks
Develops grip and shoulder-girdle endurance holding two bells in the rack
commonMistakes: Re-dipping too deep and turning the jerk into a fresh push press each rep
Losing rack position between reps and bleeding energy resetting it
Rushing the dip-drive timing as fatigue accumulates
